name: Beef organ / liver diet

card.summary: Eating beef liver and other organ meats for nutrients; liver is very nutrient-dense but also very high in preformed vitamin A.
card.note: Liver supplies preformed vitamin A at levels that can exceed the tolerable upper intake from a single serving; no appearance studies found.

quick.overview:
Organ meats such as liver, heart and kidney are eaten in many cuisines and are sometimes promoted by fitness influencers for their nutrient density. This entry concerns eating them for general nutrition and appearance-related goals.

No human trials found test the practice for appearance. Food-science studies have examined adding organs to ground beef patties.
quick.mechanism: Liver is described as rich in iron, copper, B vitamins and preformed vitamin A, and as very high in vitamin B12.
quick.risks: Excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A, with effects on bone, liver and the nervous system, and birth risks in pregnancy. A single slice of beef liver can exceed the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A.

lead: Offal, or organ meat, refers to the internal organs of butchered animals such as liver, heart, kidney, tongue and tripe.[1] Attitudes vary: some cultures treat it as taboo and others eat it daily or as a delicacy, and Wikipedia notes that awareness of its nutritional value has grown in places like Ireland, partly through fitness influencers.[1] People who eat beef liver and other organs for their looks describe it as a way to supply iron, B vitamins and vitamin A, nutrients tied to energy for training, skin health and general condition.[2][6]

Animal liver is described as rich in iron, copper, B vitamins and preformed vitamin A, and as very high in vitamin B12.[2] Vitamin A keeps the surface cells of the skin, eyes and mucous membranes healthy and supports immune function, and liver is among the richest food sources of preformed retinol; cooked beef liver is listed at roughly 5,000 to 21,000 micrograms of retinol activity equivalents per 100 g, depending on the sample.[6] The same liver reference states that a single 68 g slice of beef liver exceeds the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A.[2]

The practice sits within broader trends of nose-to-tail eating and meat-centred diets such as the carnivore diet, in which some followers add organs.[7][14] In the early 2020s it was popularised online by figures such as Brian Johnson, known as the Liver King, who built an audience around eating raw organ meat as part of an "ancestral lifestyle," and by physician Paul Saladino, who promotes organs within an animal-based diet; the two co-own a company selling freeze-dried organ capsules.[12][13] Shortly after Johnson's 2022 admission that he used anabolic steroids, public discussion of organ-meat diets and physique results became closely tied to that episode.[12]

Believers in the diet describe it in a chain: nutrient-dense organs supply heme iron and vitamin B12, which are linked to energy and red blood cells, and preformed vitamin A, which supports skin and mucous membranes. Proponents connect these to better training capacity, a clearer complexion and a healthier look. Published research has so far studied the individual nutrients far more than organ-meat eating as a pattern, and no human study has tested an organ-meat or liver diet for appearance outcomes.

paras: Edible offal includes liver, heart, kidney, tongue, tripe, sweetbreads and blood, eaten in forms from pâté and sausage to stews and grilled skewers.[1] Wikipedia notes the word derives from Germanic roots meaning 'off-fall', the parts that fall off during butchering.[1] Beef organs are the focus of this entry, and liver is the most discussed.[2]
Fitness influencers have promoted organs as a nutrient source in recent years.[1]

In medieval England, 'umble pie' made from innards was a peasant food and gave rise to the phrase 'eating humble pie', and the poor of eighteenth and nineteenth century Ireland relied on offal because they could not afford prized cuts.[1] Traditional dishes span the world, including steak and kidney pie and liver with onions in Britain, Peruvian anticuchos made with beef heart, Italian lampredotto, Spanish morcilla, and Chinese and Korean offal dishes.[1]

Chef Fergus Henderson's cookbook Nose to Tail Eating, first published in England in 1999 and reissued in the United States as The Whole Beast in 2004 with a foreword by Anthony Bourdain, made whole-animal cooking a restaurant-world talking point. Its central idea is that using the whole animal is a matter of respect.[14]

Ireland exports large volumes of offal, about 134 million euro in 2022 by Wikipedia's account, and domestic consumption is rising as people learn of its nutritional value, a message partly spread by fitness influencers.[1] Carnivore and animal-based diets, promoted on social media since 2018 by figures such as Shawn Baker and later Paul Saladino, include offal for some adherents, while Wikipedia's carnivore diet article does not describe a specific role for organ meat.[7] Dietetic bodies such as the British Dietetic Association classify the carnivore diet as a fad diet and critics cite cholesterol, fibre and micronutrient concerns.[7]

Brian Johnson, born in 1978 and raised in Texas, is an internet personality who went viral in 2021 promoting an "ancestral lifestyle" built on nine "ancestral tenets," including demanding training and large amounts of raw, unprocessed meat and organs, particularly liver, which gave him his nickname.[12] He and his wife had sold fitness supplements online since 2015, with the Liver King persona promoting the business, and as of mid-2026 he had about 6.1 million TikTok followers and about 1.2 million YouTube subscribers.[12]

In late 2022 leaked emails showed he had spent more than 11,000 dollars a month on steroids and other performance drugs, after he had repeatedly denied using them. He apologised in a video for misleading viewers and said he took roughly 120 mg of testosterone weekly.[12] Some followers sued for 25 million dollars alleging deception; the suit was later discontinued.[12] In the 2025 Netflix documentary Untold: The Liver King, he said he was wrong to have promoted the carnivore diet.[12] Medical professionals quoted on Wikipedia criticised his message that a physique like his could be reached by natural means alone, and noted the saturated fat in his recommended diet.[12] Followers and critics alike have since discussed his case as an example of how much of an influencer's physique may come from sources other than food.

Paul Saladino, a psychiatrist who earned his MD in 2015, published The Carnivore Code in 2020 and became a leading voice for meat-only eating, then moved by 2020 to an animal-based diet that adds fruit and honey after reporting side effects such as sleep problems and lower testosterone.[13] He promotes organ meats for immunity, gut health and bone strength, collaborated with the Los Angeles grocery chain Erewhon on a smoothie containing beef organs in 2023, and founded the Austin-based supplement company Heart & Soil, which sells encapsulated organ products and is co-owned with Brian Johnson.[13]

Critics cited on Wikipedia, including McGill University science communicator Joe Schwarcz, say Saladino exaggerates risks from some studies and dismisses vegetables with documented benefits; Wikipedia characterises some of his health claims as pseudoscientific.[13] Saladino and his supporters report improvements in energy and skin conditions such as his own eczema.[13]

Wikipedia lists raw pork liver as providing about 134 kcal and 21 g of protein per 100 g, with high iron and riboflavin, and notes that liver nutrients vary among species.[2] Liver is the food in which vitamin B12 was linked to its discovery.[2]

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble nutrient: preformed retinol comes from animal foods such as liver, cod liver oil, dairy and eggs, while plant foods supply carotenoids the body converts less efficiently.[6] In the eye it combines with opsin to form rhodopsin, and it supports healthy epithelial tissue, with deficiency making skin and mucous membranes dry and fragile.[6] The US adult RDA is 900 micrograms RAE for men and 700 for women.[6] Cooked beef liver is listed in the vitamin A reference at roughly 4,970 to 21,145 micrograms RAE per 100 g, the highest of the foods tabulated apart from cod liver oil.[6]

Liver also supplies copper. Wikipedia's article on copper toxicity describes chronic excess as damaging the liver and kidneys, and it concerns mainly inherited conditions such as Wilson's disease, contaminated water and copper cookware rather than ordinary diets.[15]

Hypervitaminosis A is toxicity from too much preformed vitamin A, which can come from liver, supplements and some prescription drugs.[3] Reported effects include headache and raised intracranial pressure, bone pain and fractures, skin and hair changes and liver damage, with children especially sensitive.[3] The US Institute of Medicine sets a tolerable upper level of 3,000 micrograms per day for adults, and the European Food Safety Authority uses the same figure.[3][6] The US figure was based on birth-defect risk in pregnancy; the committee considered bone-density effects but set them aside because human evidence was contradictory.[6] Wikipedia says that excess vitamin A in pregnancy can harm babies,[2] and that possible pregnancy and liver disease are reasons for close monitoring of vitamin A.[3]

Historical accounts describe poisoning from polar bear liver, with an estimated acute toxic dose of about 500 g for a human.[3] Some liver from other species carries other risks, such as mercury in ringed seal liver.[2]

Retinol carries a toxicity risk at high doses, causing liver damage, birth defects and, in infants, bulging fontanelles, whereas beta-carotene does not cause vitamin A toxicity and its excess only causes harmless orange skin discoloration.[6] Because the liver stores vitamin A, deficiency or excess may take time to appear.[6]

sections.h: Nutrients and how they relate to appearance

paras: Heme iron, found in red meat and organs, is absorbed more easily than the non-heme iron in plant foods, and its uptake is not hindered by medications or other food components.[10] Iron deficiency is described as causing fatigue, pale skin and shortness of breath, with hair thinning and brittle or grooved nails among the less common signs, and symptoms can show up before anaemia develops.[10] Pork liver is among the richest heme sources listed.[10] Women of reproductive age, teenage girls, frequent blood donors and endurance athletes are among the groups described as being at higher risk of low iron.[10] This is the line proponents draw between eating liver and having energy to train and a less washed-out appearance.

Wikipedia's heme iron article notes that high intake of heme iron from meat has been associated with higher colorectal cancer risk in a 2018 AICR/WCRF report, which described the evidence as limited but suggestive, and with breast cancer risk in a 2019 review; these are reported associations rather than established causes.[16]

Liver and other organ meats from beef, lamb, veal and turkey are listed among the richest dietary sources of vitamin B12, alongside shellfish.[11] Deficiency is described as causing fatigue, pale skin, numbness and tingling, memory problems and megaloblastic anaemia.[11] The US recommended intake for adults is 2.4 micrograms per day, and no tolerable upper intake level has been set because no harm from high intakes has been demonstrated in humans.[11] Absorption depends on stomach acid and intrinsic factor, so people with absorption disorders or who take acid-suppressing drugs are described as being at particular risk of low B12.[11]

Preformed vitamin A (retinol) is the form found in liver, and the body uses it to maintain epithelial tissue such as skin and the lining of the eyes and gut.[6] Retinoid medicines used in dermatology are chemical relatives of this nutrient, which is one reason liver is often mentioned in skin-focused diet discussions. Oral isotretinoin, a retinoid drug, is used for severe acne at doses of milligrams per kilogram, reduces sebum output by about 90 percent within one to two months in the cited figures, and is a known teratogen carrying boxed warnings.[6] Eating dietary vitamin A is not the same as taking a retinoid drug, and no trial has tested liver as an acne or skin treatment.

People who include organs in their diets describe several approaches: cooking liver, heart or kidney as regular dishes, mixing small amounts of ground organ into minced beef, eating organs raw as the Liver King persona does, or taking freeze-dried organ capsules marketed as 'nature's multivitamin'.[12][13] Food-science researchers have tested the blending approach, finding that ground beef patties containing heart, kidney or liver at 6 and 12 percent could be produced and rated by consumers, which is a sensory study rather than a health trial.[4][5] Proponents of the carnivore diet and nose-to-tail eating often present organs as the nutritional anchor of a meat-based diet.[7]

No studies found testing a beef organ or liver diet for appearance or body composition in people. Related food-science research has examined the quality and consumer acceptability of ground beef patties made with beef heart, kidney or liver at inclusion levels of 6 and 12 percent, which are laboratory and sensory studies rather than health trials.[4][5]

On T Nation, a strength-training forum, members discuss grass-fed and organic beef as part of muscle-building diets, and one member says organ meats are among her favourite foods, noting they can be expensive.[8][9] Mentions are conversational rather than formal protocols.

Organ meat also appears in appearance-culture conversation through the Liver King episode: his raw-liver routine became a widely shared symbol of "natural" muscle-building, and the 2022 steroid disclosure turned it into a frequent reference point in discussions of what diet can and cannot change about a physique.[12]

timeline.event: Poor households in Ireland rely on offal as an affordable food.[1]
German writer Bernard Moncriff publishes a book on an exclusively animal diet.[7]
Fergus Henderson's Nose to Tail Eating is first published in England.[14]
Brian Johnson and his wife begin selling supplements online; Paul Saladino receives his MD.[12][13]
Shawn Baker promotes the carnivore diet on social media.[7]
Saladino publishes The Carnivore Code and shifts to an animal-based diet.[13]
Brian Johnson goes viral as the Liver King promoting raw organ meat.[12]
Leaked emails reveal Johnson's steroid spending; he apologises. Ireland exports about 134 million euro of offal.[12][1]
Saladino collaborates with Erewhon on a beef-organ smoothie.[13]
Netflix releases Untold: The Liver King.[12]

lore.intro: Organ meats appear in strength-training and meat-centred diet circles as a nutrient-dense food, discussed alongside grass-fed beef and carnivore-style eating, and through influencers such as the Liver King and Paul Saladino.[8][9][7][12][13]

claims.claim: Liver is a nutrient-dense food that fills gaps in a diet.
claims.believers: Members of diet and training communities describe organ meats as favourite foods and as part of a whole-food approach.[9][8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes liver as rich in iron, copper, B vitamins and vitamin A and very high in B12.[2]

claims.claim: The vitamin A in liver is good for skin.
claims.believers: Proponents point to vitamin A's role in skin and eye health.[6]
claims.experts: Vitamin A keeps skin and mucous membranes healthy and deficiency makes them dry and fragile; no trial tests liver for skin appearance in people.[6]

claims.believers: Some followers of meat-centred diets eat organ meats frequently.[7]
claims.experts: A single 68 g slice of beef liver exceeds the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A, and excess is linked to liver damage, bone effects and birth defects.[2][3][6]

claims.claim: The carnivore diet improves health and physique.
claims.believers: Promoters such as Shawn Baker and Jordan Peterson describe benefits of animal-only eating.[7]
claims.experts: Dietetic bodies and critics cited on Wikipedia cite LDL cholesterol, constipation and micronutrient concerns, and no controlled trials are described there.[7]

claims.claim: Eating raw organs and living ancestrally builds an elite physique.
claims.believers: The Liver King persona presented raw liver and nine ancestral tenets as the source of his build and denied drug use.[12]
claims.experts: Johnson later admitted to taking testosterone and other drugs, and medical professionals criticised the claim that such a physique is reachable naturally.[12]

claims.claim: Organ capsules are a convenient 'nature's multivitamin'.
claims.believers: Heart & Soil and similar firms market encapsulated organs as a way to get organ nutrients without cooking them.[13]
claims.experts: No published trial found tests organ capsules for appearance; vitamin A and copper content, rather than convenience, is what nutrition references flag for high-intake products.[3][6][15]

claims.claim: Heme iron from red meat and organs supports energy and complexion.
claims.believers: Proponents link iron-rich organs to training energy and a less pale look.[10]
claims.experts: Iron deficiency causes fatigue and pale skin and heme iron is well absorbed, while a 2018 AICR/WCRF report found limited but suggestive evidence that heme-iron foods raise colorectal cancer risk.[10][16]

angle.text: Followers eat liver and other organs as a nutrient-dense food, expecting benefits for skin, energy and muscle-building. The route to a better look is indirect, through nutrition and training rather than any direct effect on the face or body.
